lessons.title: स्वर · Vowels
lessons.subtitle: The 11 Hindi vowels (अ आ इ ई ...)
lessons.content:
# स्वर (Vowels)

Hindi uses the **Devanagari** script. It has **11 vowels** (स्वर), each with a short and long form for some sounds. Learning these is the first step to reading any Hindi word.

## The 11 Vowels

| Vowel | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| अ | a | अनार | pomegranate |
| आ | ā | आम | mango |
| इ | i | इमली | tamarind |
| ई | ī | ईख | sugarcane |
| उ | u | उल्लू | owl |
| ऊ | ū | ऊँट | camel |
| ए | e | एड़ी | heel |
| ऐ | ai | ऐरावत | mythical elephant |
| ओ | o | ओखल | mortar |
| औ | au | औरत | woman |

> The eleventh vowel is ऋ (ṛ), used mainly in Sanskrit loanwords like ऋषि (sage). It is rare in everyday Hindi.

## Short vs Long

Some vowels come in short/long pairs. The long form is held about twice as long:

- अ (a) → आ (ā): अनार vs आम
- इ (i) → ई (ī): इमली vs ईख
- उ (u) → ऊ (ū): उल्लू vs ऊँट

> Tip: The long vowels आ, ई, ऊ have a vertical stroke (ा, ी, ू) that the short forms lack. This visual cue helps you tell them apart.

## Pronunciation Notes

- **अ (a)**: like the 'u' in 'but' — short, neutral
- **आ (ā)**: like the 'a' in 'father' — open, long
- **इ (i)**: like the 'i' in 'sit'
- **ई (ī)**: like the 'ee' in 'see'
- **ए (e)**: like the 'e' in 'they'
- **ओ (o)**: like the 'o' in 'go'

## Reading Practice

Try reading these single-vowel words:

- आम (ām) — mango
- ईख (īkh) — sugarcane
- ओखल (okhal) — mortar
- औरत (aurat) — woman

Each word above uses only one vowel sound. In the next lesson you will combine vowels with consonants.

lessons.title: व्यंजन · Consonants
lessons.subtitle: The 33 consonants organised by articulation point
lessons.content:
# व्यंजन (Consonants)

Hindi has **33 consonants** (व्यंजन), organised into groups by where in the mouth they are produced. This organisation makes the script logical and easier to learn than it first appears.

## क-वर्ग (Velars — produced at the back of the throat)

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| क | ka | कबूतर | pigeon |
| ख | kha | खरगोश | rabbit |
| ग | ga | गमला | flowerpot |
| घ | gha | घोड़ा | horse |
| ङ | ṅa | (rare, Sanskrit loans) | — |

## च-वर्ग (Palatals — tongue behind the hard palate)

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| च | ca | चम्मच | spoon |
| छ | cha | छतरी | umbrella |
| ज | ja | जहाज़ | ship |
| झ | jha | झंडा | flag |
| ञ | ña | (rare, Sanskrit loans) | — |

## ट-वर्ग (Retroflex — tongue curled back)

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ट | ṭa | टमाटर | tomato |
| ठ | ṭha | ठग्गी | thug |
| ड | ḍa | डमरू | damaru drum |
| ढ | ḍha | ढक्कन | lid |
| ण | ṇa | (rare, Sanskrit loans) | — |

> Retroflex sounds (ट ठ ड ढ ण) are distinctive to Indian languages. Curl your tongue back slightly — these do not exist in English.

## त-वर्ग (Dentals — tongue behind the upper teeth)

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| त | ta | तरबूज | watermelon |
| थ | tha | थाली | plate |
| द | da | दरवाज़ा | door |
| ध | dha | धनुष | bow |
| न | na | नारियल | coconut |

> Tip: English 't' and 'd' are alveolar (tongue on the ridge behind teeth). Hindi त and द are dental (tongue ON the teeth). This slight difference is what gives Hindi its characteristic sound.

## प-वर्ग (Labials — lips together)

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| प | pa | पपीता | papaya |
| फ | pha | फल | fruit |
| ब | ba | बंदर | monkey |
| भ | bha | भालू | bear |
| म | ma | मछली | fish |

## Semivowels, Sibilants, and ह

| Consonant | Roman | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| य | ya | यज्ञ | sacrifice |
| र | ra | रसोई | kitchen |
| ल | la | लकड़ी | wood |
| व | va | वन | forest |
| श | śa | शहर | city |
| ष | ṣa | (rare, Sanskrit loans) | — |
| स | sa | सड़क | road |
| ह | ha | हाथी | elephant |

## Aspiration

Each group has four sounds: unaspirated, aspirated, voiced, voiced-aspirated. **Aspiration** means a puff of air:

- क (ka) → ख (kha): 'k' vs 'k' + puff
- ग (ga) → घ (gha): 'g' vs 'g' + puff
- च (ca) → छ (cha): 'ch' vs 'ch' + puff

> Hold a tissue in front of your mouth. क should barely move it; ख should make it flutter. This is the aspiration test.

lessons.title: मात्रा · Vowel Signs
lessons.subtitle: How vowels attach to consonants
lessons.content:
# मात्रा (Vowel Signs)

When a vowel follows a consonant, it is written as a **मात्रा** (vowel sign) attached to the consonant. The consonant keeps its inherent 'a' sound only when no vowel sign is present.

## The Basic Rule

- क alone = 'ka' (inherent short 'a')
- क + ा (ā sign) = का = 'kā'
- क + ि (i sign) = कि = 'ki'
- क + ी (ī sign) = की = 'kī'

## All 11 Matras

| Vowel | Matra | Consonant + Matra | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| अ (a) | (none) | क | ka |
| आ (ā) | ा | का | kā |
| इ (i) | ि | कि | ki |
| ई (ī) | ी | की | kī |
| उ (u) | ु | कु | ku |
| ऊ (ū) | ू | कू | kū |
| ए (e) | े | के | ke |
| ऐ (ai) | ै | कै | kai |
| ओ (o) | ो | को | ko |
| औ (au) | ौ | कौ | kau |
| ऋ (ṛ) | ृ | कृ | kṛ |

> Important: The matra for short 'i' (ि) goes to the **LEFT** of the consonant, but it is read AFTER the consonant. So कि is read 'ki', not 'ik'. This is the only left-attaching matra — all others go to the right.

## Reading Practice

| Word | Breakdown | Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| कमल | क + म + ल | ka-ma-la | lotus |
| नमक | न + म + क | na-ma-ka | salt |
| दूध | द + ू + ध + (none) | dū-dha | milk |
| चाय | च + ा + य | chā-ya | tea |
| सब्ज़ी | स + ब + ् + ज़ + ी | sab-zī | vegetable |

> The small mark ् under ज़ in सब्ज़ी is the **halant** (virama) — it cancels the inherent 'a' of the consonant, so two consonants cluster together. You will learn more about this in the conjuncts lesson.

## Common Mistake

Beginners often confuse:
- कि (ki) — i-matra BEFORE consonant visually
- की (kī) — ī-matra AFTER consonant visually

> Tip: कि has a small flick on the left; की has a long vertical line on the right. The long vowel gets the long line.

lessons.title: बारहखड़ी · Consonant + Vowel Combinations
lessons.subtitle: The full grid of consonant-vowel combinations
lessons.content:
# बारहखड़ी (Barakhadi)

The **बारहखड़ी** is the full grid of one consonant combined with each of the vowels. 'बारह' means twelve — the eleven vowels plus the inherent 'a'. Mastering this grid for a few consonants unlocks reading any Hindi word.

## क Barakhadi

| Consonant + Vowel | Written | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| क + अ | क | ka |
| क + आ | का | kā |
| क + इ | कि | ki |
| क + ई | की | kī |
| क + उ | कु | ku |
| क + ऊ | कू | kū |
| क + ए | के | ke |
| क + ऐ | कै | kai |
| क + ओ | को | ko |
| क + औ | कौ | kau |
| क + ऋ | कृ | kṛ |

## म Barakhadi

| Consonant + Vowel | Written | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| म + अ | म | ma |
| म + आ | मा | mā |
| म + इ | मि | mi |
| म + ई | मी | mī |
| म + उ | मु | mu |
| म + ऊ | मू | mū |
| म + ए | मे | me |
| म + ऐ | मै | mai |
| म + ओ | मो | mo |
| म + औ | मौ | mau |

## Reading Practice — Real Words

Now read these everyday words by breaking them into consonant + matra:

- नाम (nām) — name: न + ा + म
- कलम (kalam) — pen: क + ल + म
- मकान (makān) — house: म + क + ा + न
- दीवार (dīvār) — wall: द + ी + व + ा + र
- आदमी (ādmī) — man: आ + द + म + ी
- औरत (aurat) — woman: औ + र + त

> Tip: When you see a consonant with no matra, it carries the inherent 'a' (or no vowel if followed by another consonant). When you see a matra, read the consonant + that vowel sound.

## Writing Practice

Try writing these words in Devanagari:

1. **kamal** (lotus) → कमल
2. **phal** (fruit) → फल
3. **bīj** (seed) → बीज
4. **rotī** (bread) → रोटी
5. **khet** (field) → खेत

> The barakhadi takes practice. Don't rush — spend a few minutes reading each grid aloud until the combinations feel natural. The next lesson covers conjunct consonants, which combine two consonants without a vowel between them.

lessons.title: संयुक्त व्यंजन · Conjunct Consonants
lessons.subtitle: Two consonants joined without a vowel between them
lessons.content:
# संयुक्त व्यंजन (Conjunct Consonants)

When two consonants appear together without a vowel between them, they form a **conjunct** (संयुक्त). The **halant** (्) mark cancels the inherent 'a' of the first consonant, joining it to the second.

## How Conjuncts Work

- क + ् + ष + ट = क्ष (kṣa)
- त + ् + र = त्र (tra)
- ज + ् + ञ = ज्ञ (jña)
- श + ् + र = श्र (śra)

These four — क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र — are the most common conjuncts. They often have special ligated forms.

## Common Conjuncts

| Conjunct | Written | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| क + ष | क्ष | क्षत्रिय | warrior caste |
| त + र | त्र | त्रिशूल | trident |
| ज + ञ | ज्ञ | ज्ञान | knowledge |
| श + र | श्र | श्रीमान | sir |
| द + द | द्द | दद्द | (onomatopoeia) |
| ह + य | ह्य | ह्याद | hyena |
| ह + र | ह्र | ह्रदय | heart |
| क + त | क्त | भक्त | devotee |
| न + द | न्द | आनन्द | joy |
| क + ल | क्ल | क्लांत | tired |

## Special Ligated Forms

Some conjuncts have a distinct shape that doesn't look like the two consonants stacked:

- **ज्ञ** (jña) — looks nothing like ज + ञ; must be memorised
- **त्र** (tra) — has a distinctive hook on the right
- **क्ष** (kṣa) — looks like क with a modified top
- **श्र** (śra) — has a curling stroke

> Tip: These four are sometimes called the 'चार दुष्ट' (four troublemakers) because beginners struggle to recognise them. Learn them as single units, not as two separate letters.

## Reading Practice — Common Words

- **हिन्दी** (hindī) — Hindi: ह + ि + न + ् + द + ी
- **संस्कृत** (saṃskṛt) — Sanskrit: स + ं + स + ् + क + ृ + त
- **आनन्द** (ānand) — joy: आ + न + ् + द
- **पत्र** (patra) — letter: प + त + ् + र
- **मित्र** (mitra) — friend: म + ि + त + ् + र
- **नमस्ते** (namaste) — hello: न + म + स + ् + त + े

> Notice: हिन्दी itself has a conjunct (न + ् + द = न्द). By learning conjuncts, you can now read the name of the language you're learning!

## The Anusvara (ं) and Visarga (ः)

Two special marks often appear with conjuncts:

- **ं** (anusvara / bindu): a dot above the line. It nasalises the vowel: स + ं = सं (saṃ)
- **ः** (visarga): two dots after a vowel, adds a breathy 'h': अ + ः = अः (aḥ)

> In modern Hindi, ं often replaces a conjunct nasal: संस्कृत = स + ं + स्कृत (the ं stands in for न् + स). Both spellings are valid; the anusvara form is more common in everyday writing.

## Chandrabindu (ँ)

The **chandrabindu** (ँ) — moon-dot — marks nasalisation of the vowel itself:

- हाँ (hā̃) — yes
- मैं (maĩ) — I
- हँसी (h̃sī) — laughter

> Tip: ं (bindu) nasalises the following consonant; ँ (chandrabindu) nasalises the vowel itself. The difference is subtle and varies by dialect — many Hindi speakers use them interchangeably in casual writing.

lessons.title: नमस्ते · Greetings
lessons.subtitle: Common Hindi greetings and when to use them
lessons.content:
# नमस्ते (Greetings)

Hindi has several greetings, each suited to a different time of day, formality level, or relationship. Choosing the right greeting shows cultural awareness and respect.

## The Universal Greeting

**नमस्ते (namaste)** is the most common Hindi greeting. It works any time of day, with anyone, formal or informal. Literally it means 'I bow to you' — a gesture of respect.

- नमस्ते। — Hello. / Greetings.
- नमस्ते, कैसे हैं आप? — Hello, how are you?

> When greeting an elder or someone you respect, add जी (jī) as a mark of respect: नमस्ते जी।

## Time-Based Greetings

| Time | Greeting | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Morning | सुप्रभात | Good morning (formal) |
| Morning | नमस्कार | Greetings (formal, respectful) |
| Afternoon/Evening | नमस्कार | Greetings |
| Night | शुभ रात्रि | Good night |

> In everyday speech, most Hindi speakers simply use नमस्ते regardless of time. सुप्रभात and शुभ रात्रि are more common in formal or written contexts.

## Informal Greetings

Between friends and peers:

- **हैलो (helo)** — Hello (borrowed from English, very common)
- **क्या हाल है? (kyā hāl hai?)** — How are you? (lit: what is the state?)
- **कैसा है? (kaīsā hai?)** — How are you? (informal, to a male)
- **कैसी है? (kaīsī hai?)** — How are you? (informal, to a female)

## Respectful Forms

When addressing elders, teachers, or strangers, use the respectful forms:

- **आप कैसे हैं? (āp kaīse hain?)** — How are you? (respectful, to a male)
- **आप कैसी हैं? (āp kaīsī hain?)** — How are you? (respectful, to a female)

> The word **आप (āp)** is the respectful 'you'. There are two other forms of 'you': **तुम (tum)** for friends/peers, and **तू (tū)** for close intimates or children. Using तू with someone who expects आप is considered rude.

## Common Responses

- **मैं ठीक हूँ (maĩ ṭhīk hū̃)** — I am fine
- **बहुत अच्छा (bahut acchā)** — Very good
- **ठीक-ठाक (ṭhīk-ṭhāk)** — So-so / okay
- **अच्छा हूँ (acchā hū̃)** — I'm good (informal)

## Parting Phrases

- **फिर मिलेंगे (phir milenge)** — See you again
- **अलविदा (alvidā)** — Goodbye (formal, somewhat literary)
- **नमस्ते (namaste)** — Goodbye (same word as hello)
- **चलता हूँ (caltā hū̃)** — I'm leaving now (informal, said by the person going)

## Cultural Note

When greeting, Indians often join their palms together at the chest (the **añjali mudrā**) and slightly bow the head. This gesture accompanies नमस्ते and shows respect. Handshakes are also common in urban and professional settings, especially between men.

> Tip: When meeting an elder, do not extend your hand for a handshake unless they do first. Touching their feet (चरण स्पर्श) is a traditional sign of respect for elders, especially in families.

lessons.title: मेरा नाम · Introductions
lessons.subtitle: Introducing yourself and asking names
lessons.content:
# परिचय (Introductions)

Introducing yourself in Hindi follows a simple pattern. Once you know a few key phrases, you can introduce yourself, ask someone's name, and share basic information about where you're from.

## Introducing Yourself

- **मेरा नाम ... है। (merā nām ... hai.)** — My name is ...
- **मैं ... हूँ। (maĩ ... hū̃.)** — I am ...

Examples:
- मेरा नाम राहुल है। — My name is Rahul.
- मैं अनिता हूँ। — I am Anita.
- मेरा नाम सारा है, मैं अमेरिका से हूँ। — My name is Sara, I am from America.

> Hindi sentences end with the verb. The verb **है (hai)** means 'is', and **हूँ (hū̃)** means 'am'. The subject comes first, then the object/complement, then the verb.

## Asking Names

- **आपका नाम क्या है? (āpkā nām kyā hai?)** — What is your name? (respectful, to a male)
- **आपका नाम क्या है? (āpkā nām kyā hai?)** — What is your name? (respectful, to a female — same sentence, the gender shows in the response)
- **तुम्हारा नाम क्या है? (tumhārā nām kyā hai?)** — What is your name? (informal)

> The word **आपका (āpkā)** is 'your' (respectful). **तुम्हारा (tumhārā)** is 'your' (informal). Notice how Hindi marks respect through pronouns, not just the pronoun 'you' itself.

## Where Are You From?

- **आप कहाँ से हैं? (āp kahā̃ se hain?)** — Where are you from? (respectful)
- **तुम कहाँ से हो? (tum kahā̃ se ho?)** — Where are you from? (informal)

Responses:
- **मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। (maĩ dillī se hū̃.)** — I am from Delhi.
- **मैं भारत से हूँ। (maĩ bhārat se hū̃.)** — I am from India.
- **मैं जापान से हूँ। (maĩ jāpān se hū̃.)** — I am from Japan.

> The postposition **से (se)** means 'from'. It follows the place name: दिल्ली + से = दिल्ली से (from Delhi).

## What Do You Do?

- **आप क्या करते हैं? (āp kyā karte hain?)** — What do you do? (to a male, respectful)
- **आप क्या करती हैं? (āp kyā kartī hain?)** — What do you do? (to a female, respectful)

Responses:
- **मैं छात्र हूँ। (maĩ chātr hū̃.)** — I am a student. (male)
- **मैं छात्रा हूँ। (maĩ chātrā hū̃.)** — I am a student. (female)
- **मैं शिक्षक हूँ। (maĩ śikṣak hū̃.)** — I am a teacher. (male)
- **मैं शिक्षिका हूँ। (maĩ śikṣikā hū̃.)** — I am a teacher. (female)

> Hindi marks gender on many nouns and verbs. A male student is छात्र, a female student is छात्रा — the ा ending marks feminine. The verb also changes: करते (male) vs करती (female).

## Full Introduction Example

> नमस्ते! मेरा नाम विक्रम है। मैं मुंबई से हूँ। मैं इंजीनियर हूँ। आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई।
>
> Hello! My name is Vikram. I am from Mumbai. I am an engineer. Nice to meet you.

**आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई (āpse milkar khuśī huī)** — 'meeting you brought happiness' — is the standard way to say 'nice to meet you'.

## Practice

Construct your own introduction by filling in the blanks:

1. मेरा नाम _____ है। — My name is _____.
2. मैं _____ से हूँ। — I am from _____.
3. मैं _____ हूँ। — I am a _____ (profession).

lessons.title: परिवार · Family
lessons.subtitle: Family relationships and kinship terms
lessons.content:
# परिवार (Family)

Hindi has a rich system of kinship terms. Unlike English, which uses 'uncle' and 'aunt' broadly, Hindi specifies whether the relative is on the mother's or father's side, older or younger, and by blood or by marriage.

## Immediate Family

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| माँ / माता | mā̃ / mātā | mother |
| पापा / पिता | pāpā / pitā | father |
| बहन | bahan | sister |
| भाई | bhāī | brother |
| बेटा | beṭā | son |
| बेटी | beṭī | daughter |
| पति | pati | husband |
| पत्नी | patnī | wife |

> माँ (mā̃) is the affectionate, everyday word for 'mother'. माता (mātā) is the formal/literary form. The same pattern applies to पापा / पिता for 'father'.

## Grandparents

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| दादा | dādā | grandfather (father's side) |
| दादी | dādī | grandmother (father's side) |
| नाना | nānā | grandfather (mother's side) |
| नानी | nānī | grandmother (mother's side) |

> The दा- family is the father's parents; the ना- family is the mother's parents. This distinction is important in Indian families where relationships carry specific roles and obligations.

## Uncles and Aunts

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| चाचा | cācā | father's younger brother |
| चाची | cācī | father's younger brother's wife |
| ताऊ | tāū | father's older brother |
| ताई | tāī | father's older brother's wife |
| मामा | māmā | mother's brother |
| मामी | māmī | mother's brother's wife |
| बुआ | buā | father's sister |
| फूफा | phūphā | father's sister's husband |
| मौसी | mausī | mother's sister |
| मौसा | mausā | mother's sister's husband |

> This level of specificity reflects the close-knit nature of Indian joint families. Each relative has a specific role in ceremonies and family life. Children learn these terms early.

## Talking About Family

- **मेरे पिता डॉक्टर हैं। (mere pitā ḍākṭar hain.)** — My father is a doctor.
- **मेरी माँ शिक्षिका हैं। (merī mā̃ śikṣikā hain.)** — My mother is a teacher.
- **मेरे दो भाई हैं। (mere do bhāī hain.)** — I have two brothers.
- **मेरी एक बहन है। (merī ek bahan hai.)** — I have one sister.
- **हम पाँच लोग हैं। (ham pā̃c log hain.)** — We are five people.

> Notice: **मेरे (mere)** is 'my' before plural masculine nouns (भाई, पिता), while **मेरी (merī)** is 'my' before feminine nouns (माँ, बहन). This is the possessive form — you'll learn more about it in the grammar chapter.

## Asking About Family

- **आपके परिवार में कौन-कौन हैं? (āpke parivār mein kaun-kaun hain?)** — Who is in your family?
- **आपके भाई-बहन क्या करते हैं? (āpke bhāī-bahan kyā karte hain?)** — What do your siblings do?

## Sample Description

> हमारा परिवार बड़ा है। मेरे दादा-दादी, माँ-पापा, दो भाई, एक बहन और मैं — सब साथ रहते हैं। मेरे बड़े भाई इंजीनियर हैं और मेरी बहन डॉक्टर है। मैं अभी पढ़ाई कर रहा हूँ।
>
> Our family is large. My grandparents, parents, two brothers, one sister, and I — all live together. My older brother is an engineer and my sister is a doctor. I am still studying.

> The passage above uses vocabulary you've learned. Try reading it aloud — the slow, careful pronunciation will help you internalise the kinship terms.

lessons.title: संख्या · Numbers
lessons.subtitle: Hindi numbers 0–100 and beyond
lessons.content:
# संख्या (Numbers)

Hindi uses its own number system with distinct names for each number. While Arabic numerals (0-9) are common in writing, Hindi also has Devanagari numerals (०-९) used in traditional and formal contexts.

## Devanagari Numerals

| Digit | Devanagari | Name |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ० | शून्य (śūnya) |
| 1 | १ | एक (ek) |
| 2 | २ | दो (do) |
| 3 | ३ | तीन (tīn) |
| 4 | ४ | चार (cār) |
| 5 | ५ | पाँच (pā̃c) |
| 6 | ६ | छह (chah) |
| 7 | ७ | सात (sāt) |
| 8 | ८ | आठ (āṭh) |
| 9 | ९ | नौ (nau) |

## 1–10

| Number | Hindi | Roman |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | एक | ek |
| 2 | दो | do |
| 3 | तीन | tīn |
| 4 | चार | cār |
| 5 | पाँच | pā̃c |
| 6 | छह | chah |
| 7 | सात | sāt |
| 8 | आठ | āṭh |
| 9 | नौ | nau |
| 10 | दस | das |

## 11–20

| Number | Hindi | Roman |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | ग्यारह | gyārah |
| 12 | बारह | bārah |
| 13 | तेरह | terah |
| 14 | चौदह | caudah |
| 15 | पंद्रह | pandrah |
| 16 | सोलह | solah |
| 17 | सत्रह | satrah |
| 18 | अठारह | aṭhārah |
| 19 | उन्नीस | unnīs |
| 20 | बीस | bīs |

> Notice the pattern change: 11-18 end in -rah (a contraction of दस 'ten'), but 19 (उन्नीस) breaks the pattern — it literally means 'one less than twenty'. This 'one less' pattern appears again at 29, 39, 49, etc.

## Tens (10–100)

| Number | Hindi | Roman |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | दस | das |
| 20 | बीस | bīs |
| 30 | तीस | tīs |
| 40 | चालीस | cālīs |
| 50 | पचास | pacās |
| 60 | साठ | sāṭh |
| 70 | सत्तर | sattar |
| 80 | अस्सी | assī |
| 90 | नब्बे | nabbē |
| 100 | सौ | sau |

## Compound Numbers (21–99)

For numbers between tens, Hindi uses a distinctive pattern:

- 21 = इक्कीस (ikkīs) — 'twenty-one' (one over twenty)
- 22 = बाईस (bāīs) — 'twenty-two'
- 23 = तेईस (teīs) — 'twenty-three'
- ...
- 29 = उनतीस (unatīs) — 'one less than thirty'

For 30s onward, the pattern is 'X over the ten' or 'one less than the next ten':

- 31 = इकत्तीस (ikattīs) — 'thirty-one'
- 38 = अड़तीस (aṛatīs) — 'thirty-eight'
- 39 = उनतालीस (unatālīs) — 'one less than forty'

> The numbers 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 79, 89, 99 all follow the 'उन- (una-)' pattern meaning 'minus one from the next ten'. This is a quirk of the Hindi number system that takes practice.

## Hundreds and Beyond

| Number | Hindi | Roman |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | सौ | sau |
| 200 | दो सौ | do sau |
| 1000 | हज़ार | hazār |
| 100,000 | लाख | lākh |
| 10,000,000 | करोड़ | karoṛ |

> The **लाख (lākh)** = 100,000 and **करोड़ (karoṛ)** = 10,000,000 are unique to South Asian number systems. English doesn't have a single word for these — 'one hundred thousand' and 'ten million'. Indian newspapers regularly report figures in crores.

## Using Numbers

- **मेरे दो भाई हैं। (mere do bhāī hain.)** — I have two brothers.
- **यह किताब पचास रुपये की है। (yah kitāb pacās rupaye kī hai.)** — This book is fifty rupees.
- **मैं दिल्ली में तीन साल रहा। (maĩ dillī mein tīn sāl rahā.)** — I lived in Delhi for three years.

## Time and Age

- **वह पाँच बजे आएगा। (vah pā̃c baje āegā.)** — He will come at five o'clock.
- **मैं बीस साल का हूँ। (maĩ bīs sāl kā hū̃.)** — I am twenty years old. (male)
- **मैं बीस साल की हूँ। (maĩ bīs sāl kī hū̃.)** — I am twenty years old. (female)

> Notice the gender agreement: साल (year) is masculine, so a male says 'का हूँ' and a female says 'की हूँ'. You will learn more about gender agreement in the grammar chapter.

lessons.title: सरल वाक्य · Simple Sentences
lessons.subtitle: Subject-Object-Verb word order in Hindi
lessons.content:
# सरल वाक्य (Simple Sentences)

Hindi follows a **Subject-Object-Verb (SOV)** word order. This is different from English's Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order. Once you internalise this pattern, constructing Hindi sentences becomes straightforward.

## The SOV Pattern

Compare:

- **English (SVO):** I (S) eat (V) rice (O).
- **Hindi (SOV):** मैं (S) चावल (O) खाता (V) हूँ। — I eat rice.

The verb always comes **last** in a Hindi sentence. The subject comes first, the object follows, and the verb closes the sentence.

## More Examples

| English | Hindi | Word order |
|---|---|---|
| I read a book. | मैं किताब पढ़ता हूँ। | I (S) book (O) read (V) |
| She drinks tea. | वह चाय पीती है। | She (S) tea (O) drinks (V) |
| We speak Hindi. | हम हिन्दी बोलते हैं। | We (S) Hindi (O) speak (V) |
| They go home. | वे घर जाते हैं। | They (S) home (O) go (V) |
| He writes a letter. | वह पत्र लिखता है। | He (S) letter (O) writes (V) |

## The Verb 'to be' — हूँ, है, हैं

The present tense of 'to be' has three forms based on person and number:

| Pronoun | Verb form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | हूँ (hū̃) | मैं छात्र हूँ। — I am a student. |
| तुम (you, informal) | हो (ho) | तुम दोस्त हो। — You are a friend. |
| आप (you, respectful) | हैं (hain) | आप शिक्षक हैं। — You are a teacher. |
| वह (he/she) | है (hai) | वह डॉक्टर है। — He/She is a doctor. |
| हम (we) | हैं (hain) | हम भारतीय हैं। — We are Indian. |
| वे (they) | हैं (hain) | वे लोग हैं। — They are people. |

> Notice: आप, हम, and वे all use **हैं** (hain). The plural/respectful form of the verb is the same for all three.

## Simple Statements

Build sentences using this template: **[Subject] [Object/Complement] [Verb]**

- मैं + भारतीय + हूँ = मैं भारतीय हूँ। (I am Indian.)
- यह + मेरी + किताब + है = यह मेरी किताब है। (This is my book.)
- वह + मेरा + भाई + है = वह मेरा भाई है। (He is my brother.)
- हम + स्कूल + जाते + हैं = हम स्कूल जाते हैं। (We go to school.)

## Negative Sentences

To make a sentence negative, add **नहीं (nahī̃)** before the verb:

- मैं छात्र हूँ। → मैं छात्र **नहीं** हूँ। — I am not a student.
- वह डॉक्टर है। → वह डॉक्टर **नहीं** है। — He is not a doctor.
- हम जाते हैं। → हम **नहीं** जाते हैं। — We do not go.

> **नहीं** is the standard negation word. It comes immediately before the verb. You'll learn another negation word, **न (na)**, in the next lesson — it's used in specific contexts.

## Question Words

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| क्या (kyā) | what | यह क्या है? — What is this? |
| कौन (kaun) | who | वह कौन है? — Who is he? |
| कहाँ (kahā̃) | where | आप कहाँ जाते हैं? — Where do you go? |
| कब (kab) | when | वह कब आएगा? — When will he come? |
| कैसे (kaīse) | how | आप कैसे हैं? — How are you? |
| क्यों (kyõ) | why | आप क्यों जाते हैं? — Why do you go? |

> Question words typically go right after the subject: [Subject] [Question word] [Object] [Verb]. So 'Where do you go?' is आप (you) कहाँ (where) जाते हैं (go).

## Yes/No Questions

To form a yes/no question, put **क्या (kyā)** at the start:

- वह डॉक्टर है। → **क्या** वह डॉक्टर है? — Is he a doctor?
- आप भारतीय हैं। → **क्या** आप भारतीय हैं? — Are you Indian?
- तुम जाते हो। → **क्या** तुम जाते हो? — Do you go?

## Practice

Convert these English sentences to Hindi (SOV order):

1. I am a teacher. → मैं शिक्षक हूँ।
2. She is my sister. → वह मेरी बहन है।
3. We eat food. → हम खाना खाते हैं।
4. They are friends. → वे दोस्त हैं।
5. Is this a book? → क्या यह किताब है?

lessons.title: प्रश्न · Questions
lessons.subtitle: Asking questions with क्या, कौन, कहाँ, कब, कैसे, क्यों
lessons.content:
# प्रश्न (Questions)

Hindi questions use question words that you already know from the simple sentences lesson. This lesson deepens your understanding by showing how each question word works in context, with natural conversational examples.

## क्या (What)

**क्या** asks about things and actions. It has two uses:

**As a question word (what):**
- यह क्या है? — What is this?
- आप क्या करते हैं? — What do you do?
- तुम्हारा नाम क्या है? — What is your name?
- यह किताब क्या है? — What is this book?

**As a yes/no marker (placed at the start):**
- क्या आप भारतीय हैं? — Are you Indian?
- क्या वह आएगा? — Will he come?
- क्या मैं जा सकता हूँ? — Can I go?

> The two uses of क्या look similar but function differently. As a question word, it appears where 'what' would in English (but remember SOV order). As a yes/no marker, it always comes first.

## कौन (Who)

**कौन** asks about people:

- वह कौन है? — Who is he/she?
- आप कौन हैं? — Who are you?
- वे कौन हैं? — Who are they?
- यह लड़का कौन है? — Who is this boy?

> कौन changes form based on the case: कौन (subject) → किस (oblique, singular) → किन (oblique, plural). You'll learn the oblique forms in the grammar chapter. For now, use कौन for subjects.

## कहाँ (Where)

**कहाँ** asks about place:

- आप कहाँ जाते हैं? — Where do you go?
- आप कहाँ से हैं? — Where are you from?
- बाज़ार कहाँ है? — Where is the market?
- मेरी किताब कहाँ है? — Where is my book?

> कहाँ + से = 'from where'. The postposition से (from) follows the question word: कहाँ से (from where), just as it follows place names: दिल्ली से (from Delhi).

## कब (When)

**कब** asks about time:

- आप कब आएँगे? — When will you come?
- वह कब गया? — When did he go?
- कब खाना खाएँगे? — When will we eat?
- त्योहार कब है? — When is the festival?

## कैसे (How)

**कैसे** asks about manner or state:

- आप कैसे हैं? — How are you? (to a male)
- आप कैसी हैं? — How are you? (to a female)
- यह कैसे हुआ? — How did this happen?
- मैं कैसे जाऊँ? — How should I go?
- खाना कैसा था? — How was the food?

> कैसे changes to match gender: कैसे (masculine plural / respectful), कैसी (feminine), कैसा (masculine singular). The form depends on what is being described.

## क्यों (Why)

**क्यों** asks about reasons:

- आप क्यों जाते हैं? — Why do you go?
- वह क्यों रोता है? — Why does he cry?
- यह क्यों हुआ? — Why did this happen?
- मैं यह क्यों करूँ? — Why should I do this?

> The response to क्यों usually starts with **क्योंकि (kyõki)** — 'because': क्योंकि मुझे काम है। — 'Because I have work.'

## कितना (How much / How many)

**कितना** asks about quantity. It changes form based on gender and number:

- यह कितने का है? — How much does this cost?
- आपके कितने भाई हैं? — How many brothers do you have?
- चाय में कितनी चीनी डालूँ? — How much sugar should I put in the tea?
- यह कितना बड़ा है? — How big is this?

## Conversational Examples

> **राहुल:** नमस्ते! आप कहाँ से हैं?
> **सारा:** मैं अमेरिका से हूँ। और आप?
> **राहुल:** मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। आप भारत में कब आए?
> **सारा:** मैं हफ़्ते भर पहले आई।
> **राहुल:** आपको भारत कैसा लग रहा है?
> **सारा:** बहुत अच्छा! लोग बहुत मददगार हैं।

**Translation:**
> Rahul: Hello! Where are you from?
> Sara: I'm from America. And you?
> Rahul: I'm from Delhi. When did you come to India?
> Sara: I came a week ago.
> Rahul: How does India seem to you?
> Sara: Very good! People are very helpful.

## Practice

Form questions for these answers:

1. Answer: मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। → Question: आप कहाँ से हैं?
2. Answer: मैं शिक्षक हूँ। → Question: आप क्या करते हैं?
3. Answer: वह कल आएगा। → Question: वह कब आएगा?
4. Answer: खाना बहुत अच्छा था। → Question: खाना कैसा था?

lessons.title: निषेध · Negation
lessons.subtitle: नहीं, न, मत — three ways to say no
lessons.content:
# निषेध (Negation)

Hindi has three negation words, each used in different contexts. Choosing the right one makes your Hindi sound natural.

## नहीं (nahī̃) — The Standard Negation

**नहीं** is the most common negation word. It negates statements and questions in the present and future tenses. Place it immediately before the verb.

- मैं जाता हूँ। → मैं **नहीं** जाता। — I don't go.
- वह डॉक्टर है। → वह डॉक्टर **नहीं** है। — He is not a doctor.
- हम खाते हैं। → हम **नहीं** खाते। — We don't eat.
- क्या आप आएँगे? → **नहीं**, मैं नहीं आऊँगा। — No, I won't come.

> When negating a sentence with हूँ/है/हैं, the verb often drops in casual speech: 'वह डॉक्टर नहीं' is just as natural as 'वह डॉक्टर नहीं है'.

## न (na) — Emphatic or Literary Negation

**न** is shorter and more emphatic. It appears in:

**Fixed expressions:**
- **न जाने** — who knows / heaven knows (न जाने कहाँ गया — who knows where he went)
- **न ही** — neither...nor (न ही वह आया न ही उसने फोन किया — he neither came nor called)
- **न तो...न ही** — neither...nor (न तो यह न ही वह — neither this nor that)

**Poetic or formal contexts:**
- न मैं थकता, न मैं रुकता। — Neither do I tire, nor do I stop.

**Double negation (for emphasis):**
- उसे **न** पता **नहीं** था। — He didn't know at all. (lit: he neither knew nor not-knew — used for strong emphasis)

> In everyday speech, stick to नहीं. न is more common in writing, songs, and formal speech. Using न in casual conversation can sound stilted.

## मत (mat) — Prohibitive Negation

**मत** is used for negative commands and requests — telling someone NOT to do something:

- **जाना मत!** — Don't go!
- **चिंता मत करो।** — Don't worry.
- **यह मत खाओ।** — Don't eat this.
- **रोना मत।** — Don't cry.
- **बैठो मत।** — Don't sit. (less common — usually phrased as खड़े रहो 'stand up')

> मत comes AFTER the verb in imperative sentences, or before it for emphasis. The verb is in the imperative form (without है/हूँ): जाओ → जाना मत or मत जाओ.

## Comparing the Three

| Negation | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| नहीं | Statements, questions (present/future) | मैं नहीं जाता। — I don't go. |
| न | Emphatic, literary, fixed expressions | न जाने क्या होगा। — Who knows what will happen. |
| मत | Commands, requests (don't do it!) | रोना मत। — Don't cry. |

## Negative Responses

To answer a question negatively:

- **क्या आप भारतीय हैं?** → **नहीं, मैं अमेरिकी हूँ।** — Are you Indian? No, I'm American.
- **क्या वह आएगा?** → **नहीं, वह नहीं आएगा।** — Will he come? No, he won't come.

> You can answer just **नहीं** by itself for a simple 'no'.

## Negative Questions

Negative questions express surprise or expectation:

- **क्या आप नहीं जाएँगे?** — Aren't you going? (I expected you to)
- **आप नहीं खाओगे?** — Won't you eat?
- **वह अभी तक नहीं आया?** — Hasn't he come yet?

## Common Negative Phrases

- **पता नहीं** — don't know / no idea
- **कोई बात नहीं** — no problem / never mind
- **कहीं नहीं** — nowhere
- **कभी नहीं** — never
- **कुछ नहीं** — nothing
- **बस, और कुछ नहीं** — that's all, nothing else

> **कभी नहीं (kabhī nahī̃)** — 'never' — combines कभी (ever) with नहीं. This is the standard way to say 'never'. Similarly: कहीं नहीं (nowhere), कोई नहीं (nobody).

## Practice

Negate these sentences:

1. मैं जाता हूँ। → मैं नहीं जाता।
2. वह डॉक्टर है। → वह डॉक्टर नहीं है।
3. खाओ। → मत खाओ। (Don't eat.)
4. हम खेलते हैं। → हम नहीं खेलते।

lessons.title: दैनिक दिनचर्या · Daily Routine
lessons.subtitle: Talking about everyday activities
lessons.content:
# दैनिक दिनचर्या (Daily Routine)

This lesson brings together vocabulary for everyday activities and shows how to describe a typical day. The sentences use the present habitual tense (वर्तमान काल), which describes regular, repeated actions.

## Morning Activities

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| सुबह उठना | subah uṭhnā | to wake up in the morning |
| दाँत ब्रश करना | dā̃̄ṭ braś karnā | to brush teeth |
| नहाना | nahānā | to bathe |
| चाय पीना | cāy pīnā | to drink tea |
| नाश्ता करना | nāśtā karnā | to have breakfast |
| पूजा करना | pūjā karnā | to pray / worship |

## Daytime Activities

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| स्कूल जाना | skūl jānā | to go to school |
| पढ़ाई करना | paṛhāī karnā | to study |
| काम करना | kām karnā | to work |
| दोपहर का खाना | dopahar kā khānā | lunch |
| आराम करना | ārām karnā | to rest |

## Evening Activities

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| शाम को घर आना | śām ko ghar ānā | to come home in the evening |
| खाना खाना | khānā khānā | to eat food / dinner |
| टीवी देखना | ṭīvī dekhnā | to watch TV |
| दोस्तों से मिलना | dostõ se milnā | to meet friends |
| टहलना | ṭahalnā | to walk / stroll |

## Night Activities

| Hindi | Roman | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| रात का खाना | rāt kā khānā | dinner |
| सोना | sonā | to sleep |
| किताब पढ़ना | kitāb paṛhnā | to read a book |
| दीपक बंद करना | dīpak band karnā | to turn off the light |

## Present Habitual Tense

The present habitual tense describes regular actions. The verb takes endings based on gender and number:

**Masculine:**
- मैं उठता हूँ (maĩ uṭhtā hū̃) — I wake up (male speaking)
- वह पढ़ता है (vah paṛhtā hai) — He studies

**Feminine:**
- मैं उठती हूँ (maĩ uṭhtī hū̃) — I wake up (female speaking)
- वह पढ़ती है (vah paṛhtī hai) — She studies

**Plural/Respectful:**
- हम उठते हैं (ham uṭhte hain) — We wake up
- वे पढ़ते हैं (ve paṛhte hain) — They study
- आप जाते हैं (āp jāte hain) — You go (respectful)

> The pattern: verb stem + ता (masc. sg.) / ती (fem.) / ते (masc. pl. / respectful) + हूँ/है/हैं.

## A Sample Daily Routine

> मैं रोज़ सुबह छह बजे उठता हूँ। फिर दाँत साफ़ करता हूँ और नहाता हूँ। सात बजे चाय पीता हूँ और नाश्ता करता हूँ। आठ बजे स्कूल जाता हूँ। दोपहर में दो बजे खाना खाता हूँ। शाम को पाँच बजे घर आता हूँ। फिर खेलता हूँ या टीवी देखता हूँ। रात को नौ बजे खाना खाता हूँ और दस बजे सोता हूँ।
>
> I wake up every morning at six. Then I brush my teeth and bathe. At seven I drink tea and have breakfast. At eight I go to school. At two in the afternoon I eat lunch. I come home at five in the evening. Then I play or watch TV. At night I eat dinner at nine and sleep at ten.

## Time Expressions

- **रोज़ (roz)** — every day / daily
- **सुबह (subah)** — morning
- **दोपहर (dopahar)** — afternoon
- **शाम (śām)** — evening
- **रात (rāt)** — night
- **आज (āj)** — today
- **कल (kal)** — yesterday / tomorrow (context determines which)
- **अभी (abhī)** — now / right now

## Describing Frequency

- **हमेशा (hamēśā)** — always
- **अक्सर (aksar)** — often
- **कभी-कभी (kabhī-kabhī)** — sometimes
- **शायद (śāyad)** — rarely / perhaps
- **कभी नहीं (kabhī nahī̃)** — never

## Talking About Time

- **कतने बजे? (kitne baje?)** — What time? (lit: how many o'clock)
- **सुबह छह बजे (subah chah baje)** — at six in the morning
- **दोपहर दो बजे (dopahar do baje)** — at two in the afternoon
- **रात दस बजे (rāt das baje)** — at ten at night

> **बजना (bajnā)** means 'to strike' (as a clock). So छह बजे literally means 'when six has struck' — i.e., at six o'clock.

## Practice

Describe your own daily routine using the template:

> मैं रोज़ सुबह _____ बजे उठता/उठती हूँ। फिर _____। स्कूल/काम _____ बजे जाता/जाती हूँ। शाम को _____। रात को _____ बजे सोता/सोती हूँ।

Replace the masculine/feminine verb endings based on your gender:
- Male: उठता, जाता, सोता
- Female: उठती, जाती, सोती

lessons.title: सर्वनाम · Pronouns
lessons.subtitle: मैं, तुम, आप, वह, यह — and their oblique forms
lessons.content:
# सर्वनाम (Pronouns)

Hindi pronouns mark three levels of respect (आप, तुम, तू) and distinguish between 'this' (proximate) and 'that' (remote). They also change form when followed by a postposition — the **oblique form**.

## Personal Pronouns

| Person | Direct | Oblique | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st sg | मैं (maĩ) | मुझ (mujh) | I / me |
| 1st pl | हम (ham) | हम (ham) | we / us |
| 2nd respectful | आप (āp) | आप (āp) | you (respectful) |
| 2nd informal | तुम (tum) | तुम (tum) | you (informal) |
| 2nd intimate | तू (tū) | तुझ (tujh) | you (intimate) |
| 3rd sg proximate | यह (yah) | इस (is) | this / he-she (near) |
| 3rd pl proximate | ये (ye) | इन (in) | these / they (near) |
| 3rd sg remote | वह (vah) | उस (us) | that / he-she (far) |
| 3rd pl remote | वे (ve) | उन (un) | those / they (far) |

## The Three 'You's

Hindi distinguishes three levels of 'you':

1. **आप (āp)** — respectful, formal. Use with elders, strangers, teachers, and in professional settings. Always takes plural verb agreement.

2. **तुम (tum)** — informal, familiar. Use with friends, peers, and younger family members. Takes plural verb agreement (but refers to one person).

3. **तू (tū)** — intimate, casual. Use with close friends, younger siblings, or in prayer. Takes singular verb agreement. Using तू with someone who expects आप is **offensive**.

> When in doubt, use आप. It is always safe. Indians will tell you if they prefer तुम — but never assume.

## Proximate vs Remote

Hindi distinguishes between things/people near the speaker (यह/ये) and far from the speaker (वह/वे):

- **यह लड़का (yah laṛkā)** — this boy (near me)
- **वह लड़का (vah laṛkā)** — that boy (far from me)
- **ये लड़के (ye laṛke)** — these boys (near me)
- **वे लड़के (ve laṛke)** — those boys (far from me)

> In everyday speech, यह and वह are often pronounced 'ye' and 'vo' — but they're still written यह and वह. The plural forms ये and वे are pronounced as written.

## Oblique Forms

When a pronoun is followed by a postposition (से, को, में, पर, का), it takes the **oblique form**:

- मैं + ने → **मैंने** (I — subject of past tense)
- मैं + को → **मुझे** (to me) — note: मुझ + को contracts to मुझे
- हम + को → **हमें** (to us) — हम + को contracts to हमें
- आप + को → **आपको** (to you)
- तुम + को → **तुम्हें** (to you) — तुम + को contracts
- तू + को → **तुझे** (to you) — तुझ + को contracts
- यह + को → **इसे** (to this) — इस + को contracts
- वह + को → **उसे** (to that) — उस + को contracts
- ये + को → **इन्हें** (to these)
- वे + को → **उन्हें** (to those)

## Common Postpositions

| Postposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| को (ko) | to (recipient) | मुझे दो — give (to) me |
| से (se) | from / by / with | आपसे — from you |
| में (mein) | in / into | घर में — in the house |
| पर (par) | on / at | मेज़ पर — on the table |
| का (kā) | of (possessive) | मेरा — my (of me) |
| ने (ne) | (past tense subject marker) | मैंने देखा — I saw |
| तक (tak) | until / up to | वहाँ तक — up to there |

## Possessive Forms

The possessive ('my', 'your', 'his/her') is formed by adding का (kā) to the oblique form:

| Pronoun | Oblique + का | Possessive |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | मुझ + का → मेरा | my |
| हम (we) | हम + का → हमारा | our |
| आप (you resp.) | आप + का → आपका | your (resp.) |
| तुम (you inf.) | तुम + का → तुम्हारा | your (inf.) |
| तू (you int.) | तुझ + का → तेरा | your (int.) |
| यह (this) | इस + का → इसका | its / his / her (near) |
| वह (that) | उस + का → उसका | its / his / her (far) |

> का changes to की (feminine) or के (plural): मेरा भाई (my brother), मेरी बहन (my sister), मेरे भाई (my brothers).

## Using Pronouns in Sentences

- **मैं किताब पढ़ता हूँ।** — I read a book.
- **आप कहाँ जाते हैं?** — Where do you go?
- **वह मेरा दोस्त है।** — He is my friend.
- **मुझे चाय दीजिए।** — Please give me tea.
- **उसने मुझे बुलाया।** — He called me. (past tense with ने)

## Practice

Fill in the correct pronoun:

1. _____ घर जाता हूँ। (I go home.) → मैं
2. _____ क्या नाम है? (What is your name, respectful?) → आपका
3. _____ से मिलकर खुशी हुई। (Nice to meet you.) → आप
4. _____ को खाना दो। (Give him food.) → उसे
5. _____ भाई डॉक्टर हैं। (My brother is a doctor.) → मेरे

lessons.title: लिंग और वचन · Gender and Number
lessons.subtitle: Masculine and feminine nouns, singular and plural
lessons.content:
# लिंग और वचन (Gender and Number)

Every Hindi noun has a **gender** — masculine (पुल्लिंग) or feminine (स्त्रीलिंग) — and a **number** — singular (एकवचन) or plural (बहुवचन). Gender affects verb agreement and adjective forms, so learning a noun's gender when you learn the noun is essential.

## Gender Patterns

### Feminine Endings

Nouns ending in **-ी (ī)** are usually feminine:

- लड़की (laṛkī) — girl
- औरत (aurat) — woman (exception: doesn't end in -ी)
- चाबी (cābī) — key
- किताब (kitāb) — book (feminine despite not ending in -ी)
- गाड़ी (gāṛī) — vehicle
- रोटी (roṭī) — bread

> The -ी ending is a strong feminine signal, but not every feminine noun ends in -ी. किताब (book), आग (fire), and भाषा (language) are all feminine without the ending.

### Masculine Endings

Nouns ending in **-आ (ā)** are usually masculine:

- लड़का (laṛkā) — boy
- केला (kelā) — banana
- दरवाज़ा (darvāzā) — door
- चश्मा (caśmā) — glasses
- बर्तन (bartan) — vessel (masculine without -आ ending)

> Nouns ending in a consonant or other vowels can be either gender. You must learn the gender with the noun: घर (house, masc.), कमरा (room, masc.), सड़क (road, fem.), भाषा (language, fem.).

### Common Gender Patterns

| Ending | Usually | Example |
|---|---|---|
| -ी (ī) | Feminine | लड़की, चाबी |
| -आ (ā) | Masculine | लड़का, केला |
| -अ (consonant) | Either | घर (m), सड़क (f) |
| -आ (ā, from Sanskrit) | Either | पुस्तकालय (m, library) |

> When learning a noun, always learn it WITH its gender. Use flashcards that show 'लड़की (f)' and 'लड़का (m)'. This saves you from having to guess later.

## Number Patterns

### Masculine Plural

**Type 1: Nouns ending in -आ (ā)**

Change -आ to -े:

- लड़का (boy) → लड़के (boys)
- केला (banana) → केले (bananas)
- दरवाज़ा (door) → दरवाज़े (doors)
- कमरा (room) → कमरे (rooms)

**Type 2: Nouns ending in a consonant or other vowel**

Add -ें (no change to stem, just nasalise):

- घर (house) → घर (houses) — no change! (some speakers say घरें)
- आदमी (man) → आदमी (men) — no change!
- दिन (day) → दिन (days) — no change!

> Many masculine nouns don't change in the plural — the context and verb agreement tell you it's plural. This is called the 'zero plural' pattern.

### Feminine Plural

**Type 1: Nouns ending in -ी (ī)**

Change -ी to -ियाँ:

- लड़की (girl) → लड़कियाँ (girls)
- चाबी (key) → चाबियाँ (keys)
- गाड़ी (vehicle) → गाड़ियाँ (vehicles)

**Type 2: Nouns ending in -अ (consonant or other vowel)**

Add -एँ:

- औरत (woman) → औरतें (women)
- किताब (book) → किताबें (books)
- सड़क (road) → सड़कें (roads)

## Adjective Agreement

Adjectives agree with the noun's gender and number:

**Masculine:**
- अच्छा लड़का (acchā laṛkā) — good boy
- अच्छे लड़के (acche laṛke) — good boys

**Feminine:**
- अच्छी लड़की (acchī laṛkī) — good girl
- अच्छी लड़कियाँ (acchī laṛkiyā̃) — good girls

> The pattern: -आ (m. sg.) → -े (m. pl.) → -ी (f. sg. & pl.). Some adjectives are invariable (don't change): हर (green), साफ़ (clean).

## Verb Agreement

Verbs also agree with the subject's gender and number:

**Masculine:**
- वह जाता है (vah jātā hai) — he goes
- वे जाते हैं (ve jāte hain) — they (m.) go

**Feminine:**
- वह जाती है (vah jātī hai) — she goes
- वे जाती हैं (ve jātī hain) — they (f.) go

## Common Patterns Summary

| | Masculine Singular | Masculine Plural | Feminine Singular | Feminine Plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Noun (-आ/-ी) | लड़का | लड़के | लड़की | लड़कियाँ |
| Noun (consonant) | घर | घर | सड़क | सड़कें |
| Adjective | अच्छा | अच्छे | अच्छी | अच्छी |
| Verb (present) | जाता है | जाते हैं | जाती है | जाती हैं |

## Practice

Fill in the correct forms:

1. ___ लड़कियाँ खेलती ___। (The girls play.) → वे, हैं
2. दो ___ (किताब) मेज़ पर हैं। → किताबें
3. ___ घर बड़ा है। (This house is big.) → यह
4. ___ लड़के क्रिकेट खेलते ___। (Those boys play cricket.) → वे, हैं
5. मेरी ___ (बहन) डॉक्टर है। → बहन

lessons.title: काल · Tenses
lessons.subtitle: Present, past, and future tenses in Hindi
lessons.content:
# काल (Tenses)

Hindi has three main tenses: present (वर्तमान काल), past (भूत काल), and future (भविष्य काल). Each tense uses a specific verb pattern that agrees with the subject's gender, number, and person.

## Present Habitual (वर्तमान काल)

Describes regular, habitual actions. Pattern: **verb stem + ता/ती/ते + हूँ/है/हैं**

| Subject | Masculine | Feminine |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | मैं जाता हूँ | मैं जाती हूँ |
| वह (he/she) | वह जाता है | वह जाती है |
| हम (we) | हम जाते हैं | हम जाती हैं |
| वे (they) | वे जाते हैं | वे जाती हैं |
| आप (you resp.) | आप जाते हैं | आप जाती हैं |

**Examples:**
- मैं रोज़ स्कूल जाता हूँ। — I go to school every day. (male)
- वह चाय पीती है। — She drinks tea.
- हम हिन्दी बोलते हैं। — We speak Hindi.
- आप क्या करते हैं? — What do you do? (respectful, male)

## Past Tense (भूत काल)

The past tense has two forms: **intransitive** (subject + verb) and **transitive** (subject + ने + verb).

### Intransitive Past (no object)

Pattern: **verb stem + आ/ई/ए + था/थी/थे**

| Subject | Masculine | Feminine |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | मैं गया था | मैं गई थी |
| वह (he/she) | वह गया था | वह गई थी |
| हम (we) | हम गए थे | हम गई थीं |
| वे (they) | वे गए थे | वे गई थीं |

**Examples:**
- मैं कल बाज़ार गया था। — I went to the market yesterday. (male)
- वह घर आई थी। — She had come home.
- हम दिल्ली में रहे थे। — We had lived in Delhi.

### Transitive Past (with object)

Pattern: **subject + ने + object + को + verb past participle**

- मैंने खाना खाया। — I ate food. (male)
- उसने किताब पढ़ी। — She read a book.
- हमने चाय पी। — We drank tea.
- आपने क्या कहा? — What did you say?

> The **ने (ne)** marker is required for transitive verbs in the past tense. The verb agrees with the OBJECT, not the subject: उसने किताब पढ़ी (she read a book — पढ़ी is feminine because किताब is feminine, even though the subject 'she' is also feminine).

## Future Tense (भविष्य काल)

Pattern: **verb stem + ऊँगा/एगा/एँगे/ूँगी/एगी/एँगी**

| Subject | Masculine | Feminine |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | मैं जाऊँगा | मैं जाऊँगी |
| वह (he/she) | वह जाएगा | वह जाएगी |
| हम (we) | हम जाएँगे | हम जाएँगी |
| वे (they) | वे जाएँगे | वे जाएँगी |
| आप (you resp.) | आप जाएँगे | आप जाएँगी |

**Examples:**
- मैं कल आऊँगा। — I will come tomorrow. (male)
- वह शाम को जाएगी। — She will go in the evening.
- हम रविवार को आएँगे। — We will come on Sunday.
- आप कब जाएँगे? — When will you go?

## Tense Comparison

| Tense | Pattern | Example (I go) |
|---|---|---|
| Present | stem + ता/ती/ते + हूँ/है/हैं | मैं जाता हूँ। |
| Past (intransitive) | stem + आ/ई/ए + था/थी/थे | मैं गया था। |
| Past (transitive) | ने + stem + आ/ई/ए | मैंने खाया। |
| Future | stem + ऊँगा/एगा/... | मैं जाऊँगा। |

## Common Time Markers

**Present:**
- रोज़ (roz) — daily
- हमेशा (hamēśā) — always
- अक्सर (aksar) — often

**Past:**
- कल (kal) — yesterday
- बीते हफ़्ते (bīte hafte) — last week
- पहले (pehle) — before / earlier

**Future:**
- कल (kal) — tomorrow
- अगले हफ़्ते (agle hafte) — next week
- बाद में (bād mein) — later

> **कल (kal)** means both 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' — the tense of the verb tells you which: गया था (was) → yesterday; जाऊँगा (will go) → tomorrow.

## Practice

Convert these sentences to the tense in brackets:

1. मैं जाता हूँ। (past) → मैं गया था।
2. वह खाती है। (future) → वह खाएगी।
3. मैंने पढ़ा। (present) → मैं पढ़ता हूँ।
4. हम आएँगे। (past) → हम आए थे।
5. वे खेलते हैं। (future) → वे खेलेंगे।

lessons.title: संबंधबोधक · Postpositions
lessons.subtitle: को, से, में, पर, तक, ने — Hindi's 'prepositions'
lessons.content:
# संबंधबोधक (Postpositions)

Hindi uses **postpositions** (not prepositions) — they come AFTER the noun, not before. English 'in the house' becomes Hindi 'घर में' (house-in). Mastering postpositions is essential for building natural Hindi sentences.

## The Core Postpositions

| Postposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| में (mein) | in / into / inside | घर में — in the house |
| पर (par) | on / at / on top of | मेज़ पर — on the table |
| से (se) | from / with / by | दिल्ली से — from Delhi |
| को (ko) | to (recipient/direction) | मुझे — to me |
| तक (tak) | until / as far as | वहाँ तक — up to there |
| का (kā) | of (possessive) | मेरा — my (of me) |
| ने (ne) | (past subject marker) | मैंने — I (past) |

## में (in)

- घर में — in the house
- कमरे में — in the room
- दिल्ली में — in Delhi
- किताब में — in the book
- पानी में — in the water

**Examples:**
- वह घर में है। — He is in the house.
- किताब मेज़ पर है। — The book is on the table.
- मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ। — I live in Delhi.

## पर (on / at)

- मेज़ पर — on the table
- कुर्सी पर — on the chair
- छत पर — on the roof
- दीवार पर — on the wall
- हाथ पर — on the hand

**Examples:**
- किताब मेज़ पर है। — The book is on the table.
- बिल्ली छत पर है। — The cat is on the roof.
- चित्र दीवार पर है। — The picture is on the wall.

## से (from / with / by)

से has multiple meanings depending on context:

**From (origin/source):**
- दिल्ली से — from Delhi
- बाज़ार से — from the market
- मैं अमेरिका से हूँ। — I am from America.

**With (instrument/means):**
- कलम से — with a pen
- चाकू से — with a knife
- हाथ से — by hand

**By (agent in passive):**
- राम से — by Ram (in passive constructions)

**Than (in comparisons):**
- राहुल से — than Rahul
- आज कल से — from today onwards

**Examples:**
- मैं बाज़ार से आया। — I came from the market.
- उसने कलम से लिखा। — He wrote with a pen.
- यह वह से अच्छा है। — This is better than that.

## को (to)

को marks the recipient or direction:

- मुझे (मैं + को) — to me
- उसे (वह + को) — to him/her
- आपको (आप + को) — to you
- राम को — to Ram
- स्कूल को — to school (directional)

**Examples:**
- मुझे चाय दो। — Give me tea. (to me tea give)
- उसे पता है। — He knows. (to him it is known)
- मैं स्कूल जाता हूँ। (no को needed for motion toward)
- मैं स्कूल को जाता हूँ। (with को — emphatic, less common)

> को is used with specific recipients (मुझे, उसे, राम को) and with specific, definite direct objects. It's often omitted with indefinite objects.

## तक (until / up to)

- वहाँ तक — up to there
- सुबह तक — until morning
- पाँच बजे तक — until five o'clock
- दिल्ली तक — as far as Delhi

**Examples:**
- वह रात तक आएगा। — He will come by night. (until night)
- यह रास्ता बाज़ार तक जाता है। — This road goes up to the market.

## का (of — possessive)

का changes form based on the noun it modifies:

- मेरा भाई (merā bhāī) — my brother (m. sg.)
- मेरी बहन (merī bahan) — my sister (f. sg.)
- मेरे भाई (mere bhāī) — my brothers (m. pl.)
- राम का घर (rām kā ghar) — Ram's house (m. sg.)
- राम की किताब (rām kī kitāb) — Ram's book (f. sg.)
- राम के घर (rām ke ghar) — Ram's houses (m. pl.)

> का agrees with the noun it PRECEDES (the thing possessed), not with the possessor. So 'Ram's book' = राम की किताब — की is feminine because किताब is feminine, even though Ram is male.

## ने (past tense subject marker)

ने marks the subject of transitive verbs in the past tense:

- मैं + ने → मैंने — I (past, transitive)
- वह + ने → उसने — he/she (past, transitive)
- हम + ने → हमने — we (past, transitive)
- आप + ने → आपने — you (past, transitive)

**Examples:**
- मैंने खाना खाया। — I ate food.
- उसने किताब पढ़ी। — She read a book.
- हमने चाय पी। — We drank tea.

> ने is ONLY used with transitive verbs in the past tense. Intransitive verbs (जाना, आना, सोना) don't use ने: मैं गया (I went), NOT मैंने गया.

## Compound Postpositions

Hindi also has compound postpositions formed by combining simple ones:

- के पास (ke pās) — near / with (possession): मेरे पास किताब है — I have a book
- के लिए (ke lie) — for: यह तुम्हारे लिए है — this is for you
- के बाद (ke bād) — after: खाने के बाद — after eating
- के पहले (ke pehle) — before: खाने के पहले — before eating
- के ऊपर (ke ūpar) — above: घर के ऊपर — above the house
- के नीचे (ke nīce) — below: मेज़ के नीचे — under the table
- के साथ (ke sāth) — with (accompaniment): मेरे साथ — with me
- के बिना (ke binā) — without: पानी के बिना — without water

## Practice

Translate to Hindi:

1. in the house → घर में
2. on the table → मेज़ पर
3. from Delhi → दिल्ली से
4. to me → मुझे
5. until morning → सुबह तक
6. Ram's book → राम की किताब
7. I ate (past transitive) → मैंने खाया
8. under the chair → कुर्सी के नीचे

lessons.content:
# संवाद (Conversations)

This lesson presents three dialogues that bring together everything you've learned so far. Read them aloud to practise pronunciation, then try to act them out with a partner.

## Dialogue 1: Meeting a New Neighbour

> **राहुल:** नमस्ते जी! मैं राहुल, यहाँ पास वाले फ्लैट में रहता हूँ।
> **श्रीमती शर्मा:** नमस्ते! मैं शर्मा हूँ, यह मेरा पति है। आप यहाँ नए हैं?
> **राहुल:** जी हाँ, मैं हफ़्ते भर पहले शिफ्ट हुआ। मुंबई से आया हूँ।
> **श्रीमती शर्मा:** अरे, मुंबई से! वहाँ कैसा रहा?
> **राहुल:** बहुत अच्छा, पर नौकरी के कारण दिल्ली आना पड़ा। आप लोग कब से यहाँ हैं?
> **श्रीमती शर्मा:** पिछले बीस साल से। यह हमारा अपना घर है। कुछ चाहिए तो बताइएगा।
> **राहुल:** धन्यवाद! ज़रूर बताऊँगा।

**Translation:**
> Rahul: Hello! I'm Rahul, I live in the flat nearby.
> Mrs. Sharma: Hello! I'm Sharma, this is my husband. Are you new here?
> Rahul: Yes, I moved a week ago. I came from Mumbai.
> Mrs. Sharma: Oh, from Mumbai! How was it there?
> Rahul: Very good, but I had to come to Delhi because of work. How long have you been here?
> Mrs. Sharma: For twenty years. This is our own house. If you need anything, let us know.
> Rahul: Thank you! I will.

## Dialogue 2: At the Vegetable Shop

> **विक्रम:** भैया, टमाटर कैसे दिए?
> **दुकानदार:** बीस रुपये किलो, साबित।
> **विक्रम:** थोड़ा महँगा है। पच्चीस में दो किलो दो।
> **दुकानदार:** नहीं भैया, वह नहीं होगा। ले लो, तीस में दो किलो।
> **विक्रम:** ठीक है, दो किलो टमाटर दो। और आलू भी एक किलो। आलू कितने का?
> **दुकानदार:** आलू दस रुपये किलो।
> **विक्रम:** तो चालीस रुपये हुए। यह रहे पचास, बाकी दो।
> **दुकानदार:** यह रहे दस रुपये। कुछ और?
> **विक्रम:** नहीं, बस इतना ही। धन्यवाद!

**Translation:**
> Vikram: Brother, how much are the tomatoes?
> Shopkeeper: Twenty rupees a kilo, fixed.
> Vikram: That's a bit expensive. Give two kilos for twenty-five.
> Shopkeeper: No brother, that won't work. Take it, two kilos for thirty.
> Vikram: OK, give two kilos of tomatoes. And one kilo of potatoes too. How much are potatoes?
> Shopkeeper: Potatoes are ten rupees a kilo.
> Vikram: So that's forty rupees. Here's fifty, give the change.
> Shopkeeper: Here's ten rupees. Anything else?
> Vikram: No, just this. Thanks!

## Dialogue 3: Planning a Trip

> **प्रिया:** रविवार को क्या कर रहे हो?
> **अमित:** कुछ ख़ास नहीं। क्यों?
> **प्रिया:** आगरा चलें? ताजमहल देखने?
> **अमित:** बढ़िया आइडिया! कैसे जाएँ — ट्रेन से या कार से?
> **प्रिया:** कार से चलेंगे तो रास्ते में मथुरा भी देख सकते हैं।
> **अमित:** सही कहा। कब निकलें?
> **प्रिया:** सुबह छह बजे। दस बजे तक आगरा पहुँच जाएँगे।
> **अमित:** और खाना?
> **प्रिया:** रास्ते में कहीं रुकेंगे। तुम चलने के लिए तैयार हो?
> **अमित:** हाँ, मैं तैयार रहूँगा। रविवार सुबह छह बजे मिलते हैं।

**Translation:**
> Priya: What are you doing on Sunday?
> Amit: Nothing special. Why?
> Priya: Shall we go to Agra? To see the Taj Mahal?
> Amit: Great idea! How should we go — by train or by car?
> Priya: If we go by car, we can also see Mathura on the way.
> Amit: Right. When should we leave?
> Priya: At six in the morning. We'll reach Agra by ten.
> Amit: And food?
> Priya: We'll stop somewhere on the way. Are you ready to go?
> Amit: Yes, I'll be ready. Let's meet Sunday at six in the morning.

## Key Patterns in the Dialogues

1. **Respectful address:** जी added after names; भैया (brother) for shopkeepers
2. **Bargaining:** Price negotiation is expected at markets — fixed prices are rare
3. **Suggestions with चलें?** — 'shall we go/do?' (literally: 'move?')
4. **Plans:** Use future tense + time markers (सुबह छह बजे, दस बजे तक)
5. **Hesitation/politeness:** थोड़ा (a little), बस इतना ही (just this much)

## Practice

Read each dialogue aloud three times. Then cover the Hindi and try to reconstruct it from the English. Finally, role-play the conversations with a partner, substituting your own details (name, city, items to buy).

# अनुच्छेद पठन (Reading Paragraphs)

This lesson presents three short paragraphs on different topics. Each is followed by comprehension questions. Reading longer texts is the bridge from sentence-level to real-world fluency.

## Passage 1: मेरा शहर (My City)

> मैं जयपुर में रहता हूँ। जयपुर को 'गुलाबी नगरी' भी कहते हैं क्योंकि यहाँ की इमारतों का रंग गुलाबी है। यह राजस्थान की राजधानी है और एक बहुत सुंदर शहर है। यहाँ हवामहल, अमेर किला, और जंतर-मंतर जैसी ऐतिहासिक इमारतें हैं। हर साल लाखों पर्यटक यहाँ आते हैं। जयपुर का खाना भी मशहूर है — खासकर दाल-बाटी-चूरमा और घेवर। यहाँ के लोग बहुत मेहनती और मिलनसार हैं। मुझे अपना शहर बहुत पसंद है।

**Translation:**
> I live in Jaipur. Jaipur is also called the 'Pink City' because the buildings here are pink. It is the capital of Rajasthan and a very beautiful city. It has historical buildings like Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort, and Jantar Mantar. Every year, hundreds of thousands of tourists come here. Jaipur's food is also famous — especially dal-bati-churma and ghevar. The people here are very hardworking and sociable. I love my city very much.

**Comprehension questions:**
1. जयपुर को क्या कहा जाता है? (What is Jaipur called?)
2. यह किस राज्य की राजधानी है? (Which state's capital is it?)
3. यहाँ कौन-कौन सी ऐतिहासिक इमारतें हैं? (What historical buildings are here?)
4. जयपुर का मशहूर खाना क्या है? (What is Jaipur's famous food?)
5. लेखक को अपना शहर कैसा लगता है? (How does the writer feel about their city?)

## Passage 2: भारतीय त्योहार (Indian Festivals)

> भारत त्योहारों का देश है। हर महीने कोई न कोई त्योहार आता है। दिवाली, होली, ईद, क्रिसमस, गुरुपूर्णिमा, पोंगल, ओणम — ये सब अलग-अलग धर्मों और संस्कृतियों के त्योहार हैं, पर सब मिलकर मनाते हैं। दिवाली को दीप जलाते हैं, होली को रंग खेलते हैं, ईद को सेवइयाँ खाते हैं। त्योहारों के समय लोग एक-दूसरे को मिलते हैं, मिठाइयाँ बाँटते हैं, और खुशियाँ शेयर करते हैं। बच्चों को त्योहार सबसे ज़्यादा पसंद होते हैं क्योंकि उन्हें नए कपड़े, पटाखे, और उपहार मिलते हैं। त्योहार हमें याद दिलाते हैं कि जीवन में खुशी कितनी ज़रूरी है।

**Translation:**
> India is a country of festivals. Every month some festival comes. Diwali, Holi, Eid, Christmas, Gurupurnima, Pongal, Onam — these are festivals of different religions and cultures, but everyone celebrates together. On Diwali we light lamps, on Holi we play with colors, on Eid we eat vermicelli. During festivals, people meet each other, share sweets, and share happiness. Children like festivals the most because they get new clothes, firecrackers, and gifts. Festivals remind us how important happiness is in life.

**Comprehension questions:**
1. भारत किस चीज़ का देश है? (India is a country of what?)
2. कुछ त्योहारों के नाम बताओ। (Name some festivals.)
3. दिवाली को क्या करते हैं? (What do we do on Diwali?)
4. बच्चों को त्योहार क्यों पसंद हैं? (Why do children like festivals?)
5. त्योहार हमें क्या याद दिलाते हैं? (What do festivals remind us?)

## Passage 3: खाना और स्वास्थ्य (Food and Health)

> भारतीय खाना दुनिया भर में मशहूर है। हर राज्य का अपना ख़ास खाना है — उत्तर में रोटी-दाल, दक्षिण में डोसा-सांभर, पूर्व में मछली-चावल, पश्चिम में ढबकरा-धोकला। भारतीय मसाले भी पूरी दुनिया में जाने जाते हैं — हल्दी, जीरा, धनिया, गरम मसाला। आयुर्वेद में कहा गया है कि जो हम खाते हैं, वही हमारा स्वास्थ्य बनाता है। इसलिए सही खाना ज़रूरी है। ताज़ी सब्ज़ियाँ, फल, दूध, और साफ़ पानी — ये सब सेहत के लिए अच्छे हैं। ज़्यादा तला-भुना और मीठा खाना सेहत के लिए नुक़सानदायक है। संतुलित खाना ही सबसे अच्छा है।

**Translation:**
> Indian food is famous throughout the world. Every state has its own special food — in the north, roti-dal; in the south, dosa-sambar; in the east, fish-rice; in the west, dhokla. Indian spices are also known all over the world — turmeric, cumin, coriander, garam masala. Ayurveda says that what we eat makes our health. Therefore, eating right is essential. Fresh vegetables, fruits, milk, and clean water — all these are good for health. Too much fried and sweet food is harmful to health. A balanced diet is the best.

**Comprehension questions:**
1. भारतीय खाना कहाँ मशहूर है? (Where is Indian food famous?)
2. उत्तर भारत में क्या खाते हैं? (What do they eat in North India?)
3. कुछ भारतीय मसालों के नाम बताओ। (Name some Indian spices.)
4. आयुर्वेद क्या कहता है? (What does Ayurveda say?)
5. सेहत के लिए क्या अच्छा है और क्या नुक़सानदायक? (What is good for health and what is harmful?)

## Reading Strategies

1. **Read for gist first:** Don't stop at every unknown word. Read the whole passage once to understand the main idea.
2. **Then read for detail:** Go back and look up specific words you missed.
3. **Use context:** If you don't know a word, see what comes before and after — often the meaning is clear from context.
4. **Notice patterns:** The passages use vocabulary and grammar you've already learned. Seeing them in context deepens understanding.
5. **Read aloud:** Hindi pronunciation improves with practice. Reading aloud also slows you down, aiding comprehension.

# समीक्षा (Review)

This lesson reviews everything you've learned across all five levels. Work through each section to identify areas where you need more practice before moving on to the next stage of your Hindi journey.

## Level 0 Review: Script

**Identify the vowels:**
- आम → आ (ā)
- ईख → ई (ī)
- ऊँट → ऊ (ū)

**Identify the consonants:**
- कमल → क, म, ल
- नमक → न, म, क

**Read the conjunct:**
- हिन्दी → न + ् + द (न्द)
- पत्र → त + ् + र (त्र)

**Read these words:**
- नमस्ते (namaste) — hello
- दिल्ली (dillī) — Delhi
- भारत (bhārat) — India

## Level 1 Review: Greetings & Introductions

**Greet someone:**
- Respectful: नमस्ते जी
- Time-specific: सुप्रभात (morning), शुभ रात्रि (night)

**Introduce yourself:**
- मेरा नाम _____ है।
- मैं _____ से हूँ।
- मैं _____ हूँ। (profession)

**Ask about family:**
- आपके परिवार में कौन-कौन हैं?
- आपके कितने भाई-बहन हैं?

## Level 2 Review: Daily Life

**Form sentences (SOV order):**
- I eat rice. → मैं चावल खाता हूँ।
- She drinks tea. → वह चाय पीती है।
- We go home. → हम घर जाते हैं।

**Ask questions:**
- What is this? → यह क्या है?
- Where is the market? → बाज़ार कहाँ है?
- When will you come? → आप कब आएँगे?

**Negate:**
- Statement: मैं नहीं जाता। (I don't go.)
- Command: मत जाओ। (Don't go.)

## Level 3 Review: Grammar

**Choose the correct pronoun:**
- _____ जाता हूँ। (I) → मैं
- _____ को दो। (to him) → उसे
- _____ भाई आया। (my) → मेरा

**Mark gender:**
- लड़की (girl) → feminine
- लड़का (boy) → masculine
- किताब (book) → feminine
- घर (house) → masculine

**Form the plural:**
- लड़का → लड़के
- लड़की → लड़कियाँ
- किताब → किताबें

**Use the correct tense:**
- Present: मैं जाता हूँ। (I go.)
- Past: मैं गया था। (I went.)
- Future: मैं जाऊँगा। (I will go.)

**Apply postpositions:**
- in the house → घर में
- on the table → मेज़ पर
- from Delhi → दिल्ली से
- to me → मुझे

## Level 4 Review: Reading

**Read this passage and answer the questions:**

> आज रविवार है। मैं सुबह उठा, नहाया, और चाय पी। फिर मैंने नाश्ता किया — पराठे और अचार। दस बजे मैं बाज़ार गया। वहाँ से सब्ज़ी और फल लाया। दोपहर में खाना खाया और आराम किया। शाम को दोस्तों से मिला। हम पार्क में टहले। रात को टीवी देखा और सो गया। कल सोमवार है, फिर काम पर जाना है।

**Questions:**
1. आज कौन सा दिन है? (What day is today?)
2. लेखक ने नाश्ते में क्या खाया? (What did the writer eat for breakfast?)
3. वह दस बजे कहाँ गया? (Where did he go at ten?)
4. शाम को उसने क्या किया? (What did he do in the evening?)
5. कल कौन सा दिन है? (What day is tomorrow?)
